title: Gardner and Perry Won't Be Stopped. Australia Crush West Indies to Reach Another Women's T20 World Cup Final.
excerpt: An eight-wicket demolition at The Oval sends Australia into Sunday's final at Lord's — the same ground where they ended India's campaign four days ago. England or South Africa will be their opponent.
body:
Australia's women don't just win tournaments. They suffocate them. On Tuesday at The Oval in London, Sophie Molineux's side dismantled the West Indies by eight wickets in the first semifinal of the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026, advancing to their latest final with the ruthless efficiency that has defined their era.

Chasing a modest 126, Australia barely broke stride. Beth Mooney anchored the innings with an unbeaten 61, combining with Ashleigh Gardner in an unbroken partnership that took them across the finish line with ease. Gardner, who had already claimed two wickets with the ball, finished with 35 not out and was named Player of the Match — her second consecutive match-winning performance after the 53 off 29 balls that had knocked India out of the tournament four days earlier.

## West Indies' Collapse

The script might have been different. West Indies captain Hayley Matthews and Qiana Joseph gave their side a positive start, putting on a 47-run opening stand that suggested a score north of 140 was within reach. Matthews looked settled on 30 before her dismissal triggered a middle-order collapse that the Caribbean side never recovered from.


![The Oval — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/The_Kia_Oval_-_geograph.org.uk_-_4645561.jpg)


From a position of relative comfort, West Indies slid from a promising start to 83 for 6. Deandra Dottin and Jannillea Glasgow provided late resistance, but 125 for 7 was always going to be well below par against the tournament favourites. Australia's bowling was clinical: tight lines, disciplined lengths, and enough variation to keep the West Indian batters second-guessing.



> **""I felt like I've been pretty inconsistent, where today I was working, just making sure I was hitting the stumps as often as possible," Gardner said at the post-match presentation."**


"I felt like I've been pretty inconsistent, where today I was working, just making sure I was hitting the stumps as often as possible," Gardner said at the post-match presentation. It was an understatement. She bowled with the control of someone who knows she has the luxury of fielders placed exactly where she wants them.

## The India Shadow

For Indian cricket fans watching from the UK — and there are many — the semifinal was a reminder of what might have been. India's campaign ended at Lord's on June 28, when Perry's 56 off 38 and Gardner's unbeaten 53 chased down India's 170 with an over to spare. It was India's second consecutive group-stage exit from the Women's T20 World Cup, a repeat of the heartbreak in Sharjah in 2024.


![Sophie Molineux — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/2018%E2%80%9319_VW_v_SAS_18-09-22_Molineux_%2801%29.jpg)


The parallels are uncomfortable. In 2024, India beat the weaker teams in their group but lost to Australia and New Zealand — the two strongest. In 2026, the pattern was identical: victories over Pakistan, the Netherlands and Bangladesh, defeats to South Africa and Australia. Harmanpreet Kaur scored a blistering 56 off 27 in the final group match, but it was not enough. India's fielding was among the worst in the tournament, with dropped catches at crucial junctures costing them dearly.

Head coach Amol Muzumdar's call to "rethink" the approach has been widely reported. But the structural questions run deeper: India's middle order struggled to accelerate after strong starts from Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma, and the bowling lacked the variation needed to contain Australia's big hitters.

## What Comes Next: England or South Africa

The second semifinal takes place today (Thursday, July 2) at The Oval, with hosts England facing South Africa. England are the form team of the tournament — unbeaten in the group stage with five wins from five, powered by Danni Wyatt-Hodge's extraordinary run (282 runs in 5 innings at an average of 94) and Sophie Ecclestone's eight wickets at an economy of 5.90.


![Ashleigh Gardner — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/2020_ICC_W_T20_WC_A_v_SL_02-24_Gardner_%2802%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)


South Africa, however, are the team that beat India in the group stage and have won four of their five matches. Marizanne Kapp's all-round brilliance — 7 wickets at an economy of 5.21 — gives them genuine firepower. Tazmin Brits has been equally impressive with 174 runs in three innings at an average of 87.

The head-to-head record favours England heavily, with 17 wins from 25 T20Is between the sides. But knockout cricket has a way of levelling the field, and South Africa's run in ICC events has been building towards a breakthrough moment.

Whoever emerges will face Australia in the final at Lord's on Sunday, July 5. For Australia, it will be a shot at a record-extending seventh Women's T20 World Cup title. For everyone else — including the millions of Indian fans who will watch as neutrals — it will be a reminder of the gap that still needs to be closed.

## How to Watch

The final at Lord's on July 5 starts at 7 PM IST (2:30 PM local time, 9:30 AM ET, 6:30 AM PT). In the US and Canada, the match will be available on Willow TV. In India, it airs on Star Sports and streams on JioHotstar. In the UK, coverage is on Sky Sports.
